Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Work & responsibility

experience noun

knowledge or skill gained by doing

also know-how, practical knowledge, experienced, work experience, inexperienced

classical

Plin. Ep. 1.20.12: quod mē docuit ūsus, magister ēgregius
Cic. de Or. 2.204: docuit nōs longa vīta ūsusque rērum maximārum (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 152
Traupman 311

ūsus, ūsūs m.

noun, fourth declension

experience, practice

Often ūsus rērum, experience of affairs (M-O s.v. experience). “Experienced in” is perītus with the genitive (Traupman 152); “inexperienced”, imperītus (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • perītia, perītiae f. — experience, practical skill

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Sall. Jug. 46.8: locōrum et mīlitiae (Lewis & Short); Tac. H. 4.30 (Lewis & Short)

    Sallust and Tacitus; not in Cicero or Caesar (Lewis & Short).

  • experientia, experientiae f. — experience gained by trial

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Tac. A. 1.4: rērum experientia (Lewis & Short); Traupman 152; Traupman 311

    Classically a trial or an attempt; in the sense “experience” from Vergil (G. 1.4) and in post-Augustan prose (Lewis & Short).

  • inexpertus, inexperta, inexpertum — inexperienced (in)

    with the dative or ad + acc.; Traupman also ab, in, adversus, declension · also used · classical · Liv. 6.18.4: animus ad contumēliam inexpertus (Lewis & Short); Traupman 332

    Not in Cicero or Caesar (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Adjiciam quod mē docuit ūsus, magister ēgregius.

    I will add what experience, an excellent teacher, has taught me.Plin. Ep. 1.20.12

  • Ūsus est optimus magister.

    Experience is the best teacher.Traupman 255

See also experience, practice.
